According to the latest issue of Mark Gurman's "Power On" newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering several changes to its App Store. What's the goal? To boost the potential revenue the App Store can generate.

The specifics of Apple's App Store overhaul remain unclear. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," with the efforts being driven primarily by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

According to reports, this overhaul was one of the reasons senior staff member Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020 to take on the role of Apple Fellow, at which point part of his responsibilities included overseeing the App Store. Schiller was not in agreement with the proposals:

There are many ways Apple could improve App Store margins. For one, it could do away with the human app review process—an expensive and arguably questionable procedure in an era of automated coding. Further automating review could anger users, but it would undoubtedly save money.

Apple could also raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers spend $200 per month on Codex and Claude subscriptions to build apps, Apple is well-positioned to raise prices without much pushback. The company could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing on some of the infrastructure costs.

The end result remains to be seen, but I'm very much looking forward to seeing what these changes ultimately look like.
